title: N-vium: Mixture-of-Exits Transformer for Accelerated Exact Generation
claim: Routing tokens to shallower exits cuts the sequential depth of each decoding step, so cumulative latency grows far more slowly than the baseline.
layout: 1 panel, stepped line plot, left-to-right, shaded savings gap with double-arrow
description: A single stepped plot of cumulative latency (y-axis, 0 to about 15) against the tokens of an example sentence on the x-axis: "At every junction a wise model can pick the shortest route that is still correct". A thick black staircase is the baseline, rising by 1 per token. Beneath it, small colored boxes mark the latency of each token at its chosen exit depth: green for 25%, purple for 50%, yellow for 75% and orange for 100% depth. Together they form a much lower staircase. The light blue region between the two staircases is labeled latency savings. A vertical double-headed arrow at the right edge is labeled "50% Speedup". The legend sits below the plot in two rows. The eye goes first to the blue gap and the arrow.
caption: Illustrative example of cumulative latency of Quadrivium vs.\ a standard transformer. By early sampling, Quadrivium achieves up to 57% reduction in cumulative latency. Tokens are routed to shallower prediction heads, reducing the sequential depth of each decoding step.
abstract: Improving the inference efficiency of autoregressive transformers typically means reducing FLOPs per token, usually through approximations that degrade model quality. We introduce N-vium, a mixture-of-exits transformer that partially parallelizes computation across depth on standard hardware, increasing effective FLOPs per second rather than minimizing compute per token. N-vium attaches prediction heads at multiple depths and defines the next-token distribution as a learned mixture over these exits, with token-adaptive routing. This formulation strictly generalizes the standard transformer, which is recovered exactly when routing assigns zero mass to all intermediate heads. Sampling from the mixture is exact, and complete KV caches are recovered by deferring the upper-layer computation and batching it with later tokens. We pretrain N-vium at scales up to 1.5B parameters. Our largest model reaches 57.9% wall-clock speedup over a parameter- and data-matched standard transformer at no perplexity cost.
